name: Bowl cut

lead: The bowl cut has a straight fringe across the forehead with the rest of the hair cut to an even length, or with the back and sides cut shorter. It takes its name from the medieval habit of using a bowl as a cutting guide.

People choose it as a stylistic statement: it has been revived in the 2020s, with performer Oliver Tree a prominent wearer. Forum posts show it is also something people end up with by accident and then try to modify.

paras: A barber or home cutter shapes a rounded fringe and even perimeter. When someone dislikes the result, forum replies suggest trimming some hair shorter, adding layering, and using sea salt spray and texture powder to break up the shape.

No health risks. The social reading varies by region and era: Wikipedia says it has been ridiculed in the US since the 1980s, and that some extremist groups have used it as a symbol, so wearers may find it carries unwanted associations.

angle.text: The cut reshapes the hair outline into a rounded fringe. Wearers choose it for a distinctive style, and a texturised or layered version is used to soften the shape.

lead: The bowl cut is a simple haircut with a straight fringe across the front; the rest of the hair is either one even length all round or cut shorter at the sides and back. The name comes from the old practice of placing a bowl on the head as a cutting guide.[1]

It was common among ordinary European and Asian men partly because it could be done at home, and it peaked in Europe in the late Middle Ages, the first half of the 15th century. Attitudes differed by culture, and in some places it signalled that the wearer could not afford a barber.[1]
People use it today for a retro or fashion-forward look; Oliver Tree adopted it in 2016 and helped revive it in the 2020s.[1]

Wikipedia records local names for the style in many languages, including 'mushroom cut' in Japanese and 'flowerpot haircut' in Dutch, which reflects how widely a bowl-shaped crop has appeared [1]. In modern barbering it is also treated as a base for textured, layered or curtain-fringe variations rather than only as a literal bowl shape.
infobox: Medieval Europe; also common in Asia

paras: The classic version leaves the hair at one length around the head with a straight fringe; variants cut the sides and back short while keeping a rounded top.[1]

Wikipedia describes only two broad forms: one even length all round, or short sides and back under a straight fringe [1]. Related cuts it lists include the bob and the Edgar cut [1]. Wearers who want a softer outline generally ask a barber for added layers or texture, as the forum thread in this article shows [2].

The style was widespread in late medieval Europe. Wikipedia notes Joan of Arc had her hair cut this way in February 1429, and that the record of her 1431 trial describes it mockingly as shaved round like a fashionable young man.[1] In some places it was ordinary, and elsewhere it implied poverty because it could be cut without a barber.[1]

Wikipedia cites artworks as evidence of its late-medieval popularity, including the Bedford Hours (c. 1410-30), the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (c. 1435) and the Melun Diptych (c. 1452), and also pictures it on a 19th-century Polish peasant and in a 1920s Soviet Ukrainian poster [1]. The folk explanation that a cooking pot or bowl served as the guide is flagged in that article as needing better sourcing [1].

In the United States it was never very popular and has been widely joked about since the 1980s, often through internet memes. Wikipedia, citing the Anti-Defamation League, also notes some white-supremacist groups have used it as a symbol.[1]

Wikipedia notes that the Anti-Defamation League has documented use of the cut by some young white supremacists as a reference to Dylann Roof, who wore one at the 2015 Charleston church shooting, and that a neo-Nazi group called itself the Bowl Patrol; this association is a reason some wearers report being cautious about the style [1].

Singer Oliver Tree began appearing with a bowl cut in 2016, and the cut became his most recognisable feature as his career rose through the late 2010s and 2020s; Wikipedia says he helped repopularise the style [1][3]. His biography notes he signed to Atlantic Records in October 2016, released his debut album Ugly Is Beautiful in July 2020, and was described in coverage of Coachella fashion in 2017 as among its best and weirdest [3]. Wikipedia also cites 2019 coverage of celebrities bringing the cut back [1].

On looksmax.org, one user posted that they asked for a mod cut and received a bowl cut. Replies suggested trimming sections shorter, adding layering, and using sea salt spray and texture powder; the poster said the powder did not help and planned to try the spray.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the bowl cut mostly appears as an unwanted outcome people try to fix.[2]

claims.claim: A bad bowl cut can be rescued with layering and texture products
